subject: Denominator in the chi-squared GOF test for binary data

messages.author: 3fac8f4565858af2
messages.subject: Denominator in the chi-squared GOF test for binary data
parts:
I am trying to calculate a variety of residuals for goodness of fit (GOF) tests of an occupancy model in a Bayesian framework, and I can’t seem to find consensus on what should be in the denominator of the chi-squared test.

 

The unmarked vignette states, “Here we use a χ2 statistic appropriate for binary data:”

 

chisq <- function(fm) {

  umf <- getData(fm)

  y <- getY(umf)

  y[y>1] <- 1

  sr <- fm@sitesRemoved

  if(length(sr)>0)

    y <- y[-sr,,drop=FALSE]

  fv <- fitted(fm, na.rm=TRUE)

  y[is.na(fv)] <- NA

  sum((y-fv)^2/(fv*(1-fv)), na.rm=TRUE)

  }

Here, fv = the expected (fitted) values of y (the Expectation of y, E(y)). In the last line of this function, the variance of y (Var(y)) is in the denominator; in other words, the Var(y) = fv*(1-fv), as for a Bernoulli distribution. This differs from the function suggested in the examples under the function parboot in the unmarked reference manual (help file):

 

fitstats <- function(fm) {

  observed <- getY(fm@data)

  expected <- fitted(fm)

  resids <- residuals(fm)

  sse <- sum(resids^2, na.rm=T)

  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected, na.rm=T)

  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2, na.rm=T)

  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)

  return(out)

}

 

Here, the expected (fitted) values of y, E(y), make up the denominator. If applied to count data in a Poisson model, the mean = lambda = E(y) = Var(y) so it makes no difference as to which of these is in the denominator.

 

Inevitably, does it matter which chi-squared formulation to use? Only for a large p? For a binomial distribution, E(y) = np and Var(y) = np(1-p) and Bernoulli E(y) = p and Var(y)=p(1-p), so for a small p the variance is close to the mean E(y).

 

It looks like Mackenzie and Bailey 2004, including the AICcmodavg::mb.chisq() function in mb.gof.test.R, use E(y) in the denominator, as do Kery and Royle 2016 in their AHMbook (p. 253). So, I’m inclined to go with that. However, the occupancy model that I specified estimates a large p.

 

Therefore, I’d appreciate confirmation to my lingering question (also see here):

Which is it? E(y) or Var(y) in the denominator of the Chi-squared GOF test for binary data (in an occupancy model)?

 

Thanks,

Holly

messages.author: 3fac8f4565858af2
messages.subject: Re: Denominator in the chi-squared GOF test for binary data
parts: In response to my previous question, I'd like to offer an answer. If I am not mistaken, having Var(y) in the denominator of the Chi-squared GOF test for binary data is equivalent to the squared Pearson residual (but not the standardized Pearson residual, which is not squared). So I believe that the unmarked vignette is basically using a Pearson χ2 statistic (with Var(y) in the denominator), whereas the example under the function parboot in the unmarked reference manual (help file) is using a standard χ2 statistic (with only E(y) in the denominator).
